title: Beer, sake and spirits
lead: The basics the Court tests outside wine: what beer and sake are made from, ale versus lager, sake grades, how distillation works, and the base ingredient and key rules of each common spirit and liqueur.

intro.title: WHAT THE COURT TESTS
intro.text: The Introductory exam content list asks for these basics of each drink.

outline: Beer: Examples of ales and lagers
Spirits and Liqueurs: Basics of distillation
Spirits and Liqueurs: Base ingredient of common spirits
Spirits and Liqueurs: Basics of common spirits
court.outcome: BEER: After studying this section, a student will know what beer is, its primary ingredients and what they contribute to a beer, the difference between an ale and lager, and examples of each. | SAKE: After studying this section, a student will know what sake is, where it's from, its main ingredients, and the basics of how it is made. A student will learn a quality classification exists and will be able to recognize quality categories. | SPIRITS & LIQUEURS: After studying this section, a student will learn basics of spirit and liqueur production including the base ingredients, flavors, and location of production for important spirits of the world.

sections.name: Beer: what goes in

lines.label: Definition
lines.text: Beer is a fermented drink made from cereal grains (mainly barley), water, hops and yeast.

lines.label: Process
lines.text: The grain's starch must become sugar before it can ferment. The Court's steps are germination, malting and fermentation.

know: Malt gives sugar for fermentation, plus color, flavor, body, texture and mouthfeel.
Hops give aroma, flavor and bitterness to balance malt sweetness, and act as a natural preservative.
Yeast eats the malt sugars and makes alcohol. The type of yeast decides ale or lager.
Water is 90% or more of a beer.
Yeast can add aromas and flavors too, and the many hop varieties give a wide range of flavors and aromas.

items.text: Sugar, color, flavor, body

items.name: Hops
items.text: Aroma, bitterness, preservative

items.name: Yeast

items.name: Water

sections.name: Ales and lagers

lines.label: Ale
lines.text: Top-fermenting yeast makes ales, with more fruit and spice aromas.

lines.label: Lager
lines.text: Bottom-fermenting yeast makes lagers: clean and crisp, with less yeast effect on aroma and flavor.

know: Pilsner started in the Czech Republic; Pilsner Urquell was first brewed in Plzeň in 1842.
Irish Dry Stout is black and roasty, often like coffee; draught versions are creamy from a nitro pour.
Hefeweizen (Weissbier) is a German wheat ale with banana-and-clove yeast character.
Lambic is a sour Belgian wheat beer, fermented by wild yeast and bacteria.
Witbier is a hazy Belgian wheat ale, traditionally spiced with coriander and dried orange peel.

sections.name: Sake

lines.label: What it is
lines.text: Sake is a fermented drink made from rice, mostly in Japan. It uses special sake rice, koji, yeast and water; some styles also get brewer's alcohol.

lines.label: How it ferments
lines.text: Koji-kin is a mold grown on steamed rice that turns starch into sugar. Yeast turns that sugar into alcohol at the same time (parallel fermentation).

know: Junmai means no alcohol added.
The polishing rate is how much of the grain is left: 70% means 30% was milled away.
Ginjo and Daiginjo use low-temperature fermentation and have a fruity aroma.
Nigori is cloudy sake. Namazake is unpasteurized.
The Court gives sake as typically 15-22% ABV.

sections.name: Distillation

lines.label: What it does
lines.text: Distilling boils a fermented liquid and condenses the vapor into a stronger alcoholic liquid.

lines.label: Pot or column
lines.text: Pot stills work in batches; single malt Scotch must use copper pot stills. Column (patent or Coffey) stills run continuously; Aeneas Coffey's 1831 still led to grain whisky.

know: US vodka is neutral spirit distilled at 95% ABV (190 proof) or higher and never aged in wood.
US whisky, brandy, rum and agave spirits are distilled below 95% ABV and bottled at 40% or more.
The Court lists Irish whiskey as distilled three times in a pot still, and Scotch two times.
Cognac is double distilled in batches; Armagnac is distilled once in a continuous still.

sections.name: Whisk(e)y

lines.label: Bourbon (US law)
lines.text: At least 51% corn, distilled at 160 proof or less, stored in charred new oak barrels at 125 proof or less, with no added coloring or flavoring. It must be made in the US. Most is made in Kentucky, but that isn't required.

lines.label: Scotch (UK law)
lines.text: Made in Scotland from water and malted barley, distilled below 94.8% ABV, then matured in Scotland in oak casks of 700 liters or less for at least three years. Bottled at 40% or more.

know: Straight bourbon must age at least 2 years in charred new oak.
Tennessee whiskey is also at least 51% corn; the Court lists filtering through maple charcoal as its distinct process.
Islay is the Court's smokiest region; peat fires that dry the barley give the smoke.
A Scotch age statement refers to the youngest whisky in the bottle.
Irish whiskey is barley, distilled three times in a pot still. Canadian whisky uses corn, wheat, rye or barley, typically in a continuous still, and ages at least 3 years in oak.

sections.name: Cognac and other brandy

lines.label: Cognac
lines.text: Grape brandy distilled only in France's Cognac region, mainly from Ugni Blanc. It is double distilled in a pot still and aged in French oak; distillation must end by March 31 after the harvest.

lines.label: Age labels
lines.text: The age on the label is the youngest brandy in the blend. Cognac can't be sold before two years in oak.

know: VS: at least 2 years. VSOP: at least 4. XO: at least 10. XXO: 14 or more.
Napoléon means at least 6 years.
Fine Champagne Cognac is Grande Champagne (at least 50%) plus Petite Champagne.
Armagnac is distilled once in a continuous still. Calvados is made from apples and pears.
Grappa (Italy) and Marc (France) are pomace brandies. Like fruit eaux de vie, they are generally not aged.

Reposado: at least 2 months in oak. Añejo: at least 1 year. Extra Añejo: at least 3 years.

Cooking the agave over fire in pits gives mezcal its smoky character.

sections.name: Vodka, gin, rum and liqueurs

lines.label: Clear spirits
lines.text: Vodka is neutral spirit with no wood aging. Gin gets its main flavor from juniper. Rum is distilled from sugar cane juice, syrup or molasses.

lines.label: Liqueurs
lines.text: Liqueurs are spirits flavored with fruits, flowers, plants or other natural flavors, with at least 2.5% sugar by weight (US rule).

know: Gin made only by distillation may be labeled Distilled, Dry, London or Old Tom (US).
The Court's rum styles are light, dark, aged and spiced; rum is traditionally Caribbean but can be made anywhere.
Orange liqueurs: Triple Sec, Cointreau, Grand Marnier.
Coffee liqueurs: Kahlúa, Tia Maria. Whiskey liqueurs: Drambuie, Glayva, Irish Mist.
The Court says vodka is commonly distilled many times in a continuous still to remove flavor; gin is made in a continuous still; rum in a continuous or pot still.

facts.fact: Exam content (Introductory): beer basics (main ingredients, common styles); sake basics (ingredients, quality scale); spirits basics (base ingredients, common styles).

Course Section 11 'Important World Beverages': Beer (ingredients; ale and lager differences; examples of ales and lagers); Sake (ingredients; production basics; quality grades); Spirits and Liqueurs (basics of distillation; base ingredient of common spirits; basics of common spirits).

Beer definition: a fermented beverage from cereal grains (mainly barley), water, hops, and yeast. Grains: mainly barley plus rice, corn, wheat and oats; starch must be converted to sugar for fermentation. Malt provides sugar for fermentation plus color, flavor, body, texture and mouthfeel. Yeast consumes malt sugars to create alcohol and can add aromas and flavors; yeast type determines ale or lager. Ales: top-fermenting yeasts, more aromas such as fruit and spices. Lagers: bottom-fermenting yeasts, clean and crisp, less effect on aroma and flavor. Hops: flowering cone of the hop vine; aroma, flavor and bitterness to balance malt sweetness; natural preservative with antibacterial properties. Water: 90%+ of beer content.
Certified column: ales use Saccharomyces cerevisiae, warm fast fermentation (68-72°F / 20-22°C); lagers use Saccharomyces pastorianus, cool slow fermentation (48-55°F / 9-13°C).

Beer process (Intro): germination, malting, fermentation. Ale examples: Germany - Hefeweizen; Britain - Pale Ale, India Pale Ale (IPA), Porter; Ireland - Irish Dry Stout; Belgium - Lambic, Wit or White Ale. Lager examples: American Lager, European Lager; Czech Republic - Pilsner (origin of the Pilsner beer); Germany - Pilsner (Pils), Bock, Doppelbock, Oktoberfest.
Czech Premium Pale Lager is commonly associated with Pilsner Urquell, first brewed in 1842 in Plzeň.
Irish Stout: a black beer with a pronounced roasted flavor, often similar to coffee; draught versions are typically creamy from a nitro pour. It evolved from London porters.
Weissbier (also known as hefeweizen): pale, refreshing German wheat beer with high carbonation and a distinctive banana-and-clove yeast profile; malted wheat at least half the grist.
Witbier: pale, hazy Belgian wheat ale; traditionally uses coriander seed and dried Curaçao orange peel; revived in 1966 by Pierre Celis at what became Hoegaarden.

Lambic: a fairly sour, wild Belgian wheat beer from in and around Brussels, spontaneously fermented with naturally occurring yeast and bacteria; aged hops used more as preservative than for bitterness.
American IPA: a decidedly hoppy and bitter, moderately strong, pale American ale.

Sake (Intro): a fermented beverage made from rice; the majority of production is in Japan. Rice: special varieties (not table rice). Koji-kin: a mold that converts rice starch to sugar, sprinkled over steamed rice. Yeast converts sugar into alcohol after koji converts starch; sake is typically 15-22% abv. Water: each brewery has its own source. Brewer's alcohol: added to some styles and not others. Certified: Koji-kin = Aspergillus oryzae; parallel fermentation; Nigori = cloudy sake; Namazake = unpasteurized.

Sake classification (Intro): recognize Junmai, Honjozo, Ginjo, Daiginjo as part of the premium classification; Junmai = no alcohol added. Certified: minimum % of rice grain remaining - Daiginjo 50%, Ginjo 60%, Honjozo 70%; Junmai Daiginjo 50%, Junmai Ginjo 60%. Ginjo and Daiginjo best served chilled.

JSS glossary: Junmai - sake made without the addition of neutral spirits. Honjozo - rice polished to 70% or less plus neutral spirits up to 10% of polished rice weight. Ginjo - rice polished to 60% or less with low-temperature fermentation; fruity aroma, light flavor. Daiginjo - rice polished to 50% or less with low-temperature fermentation. Rice polishing rate is the percentage of the grain left after polishing; if 30% is polished away, the rate is 70%. Specially designated sake has 8 categories. Koji-kin is Aspergillus oryzae. Parallel fermentation: saccharification by koji and fermentation by yeast happen at the same time. Nigori: cloudy sake filtered with a coarse mesh. Namazake: unpasteurized sake. Sake is usually diluted to around 15% alcohol.

Tequila distillation: the fermented liquid is boiled and, on condensing the vapor, a concentrated alcoholic liquid is obtained; done in two phases, generally in stills, though distillation towers also exist.
In 1831 Aeneas Coffey invented the Patent Still, which enabled continuous distillation and led to grain whisky, a lighter spirit than malt whisky.
Single Malt Scotch Whisky is distilled at a single distillery from water and malted barley without other cereals, by batch distillation in copper pot stills.

Court spirits table (Intro): Vodka - anywhere in the world, commonly cereal grain but can be anything, commonly continuous still, distilled multiple times in continuous still to remove any flavors. Rum - can be anywhere but traditionally Caribbean, sugarcane and molasses, continuous or pot still. Gin - anywhere, neutral grain, continuous, flavored with botanicals and juniper berries. Tequila - Jalisco, Mexico, blue agave, continuous or pot still. Mezcal - Oaxaca, Mexico, agave (many varieties), continuous or pot still, agave cooked over fire in pits gives a smoky character. Certified (red): rum styles Light, Dark, Aged, Spiced; gin style London Dry.

Court whisk(e)y table (Intro, black text; columns read by text position Nov 2 2026): Bourbon - USA (most are made in Kentucky but not required), 51% corn, new charred American white oak. Tennessee - Tennessee, USA; 51% corn; filtered through maple charcoal. Canadian - Canada; corn, wheat, rye or barley; typically continuous still; styles/age: min 3 years in oak. Irish - Ireland; barley; three times in pot still. Scotch - Scotland; barley; subregions Highland, Lowland, Islay (smokiest), Speyside, Campbeltown; styles: single malt / blended; two times in pot still (Lowlands three times: Certified, red); peat fires dry the barley (giving a smoky character: red). A sixth column covers Blended Scotch. Producers are Certified (red).

Court brandy table: Cognac - VS/Three Star 2 years, VSOP 4 years, XO 10 years (Certified); white grapes, mainly Ugni Blanc (Certified); two times in a pot still; aged in French oak. Armagnac - one time in a unique continuous still; aged in French oak. Calvados - apples, pears; aged in French oak. Pomace brandy: Grappa (Italy), Marc (France). Calvados - two times in a pot still, some use continuous. Eaux de Vie de Fruits - France; raspberry, cherry, pear; generally no aging. Pomace brandy - generally no aging. (Intro, black text; Calvados and eau-de-vie style names are red/Certified.)

Court liqueurs and cordials table: Herb & Nut - Benedictine, B&B, Pimm's, Chartreuse, Crème de Menthe, Frangelico; Anise - Anisette, Galliano, Ouzo, Sambuca. Fruit - Orange: Triple Sec, Cointreau, Grand Marnier; Peaches: Southern Comfort; Apricot: Amaretto. Cream - Baileys Irish Cream. Whiskey - Drambuie, Glayva, Irish Mist. Other - Elderflower: St. Germain; Ginger: Canton; Coffee: Kahlúa, Tia Maria.

Neutral spirits are distilled at or above 95% ABV (190 proof) and bottled at not less than 40% ABV; vodka is a type of neutral spirits and may not be aged or stored in wood barrels (except paraffin-lined barrels for bottled in bond).

Whisky: distilled from a fermented mash of grain at less than 95% ABV, stored in oak barrels (except corn whisky), bottled at not less than 40% ABV. Bourbon: mash of not less than 51% corn, distilled at 160 proof or less, stored in charred new oak barrels at 125 proof or less; no added coloring, flavoring or blending materials. Straight bourbon: charred new oak for a minimum of 2 years. 'Bourbon' may not be used for whisky not distilled and aged in the United States. Rye whisky: not less than 51% rye.

Gin: made by distillation or redistillation, or by mixing neutral spirits, with or over juniper berries and optionally other aromatics; must derive its main characteristic flavor from juniper berries; bottled at not less than 40% ABV. Gin made only by original distillation or redistillation may be called 'distilled', 'Dry', 'London' or 'Old Tom'.

Brandy: distilled from the fermented juice, mash or wine of fruit, or its residue, at less than 95% ABV, bottled at not less than 40% ABV. Cognac: grape brandy distilled exclusively in the Cognac region of France. Armagnac: grape brandy distilled in France under French Armagnac rules.

Rum: distilled from the fermented juice of sugar cane, sugar cane syrup, sugar cane molasses or other sugar cane by-products at less than 95% ABV; bottled at not less than 40% ABV. Cachaça is rum that is a distinctive product of Brazil.
Agave spirits: at least 51% from Agave; Tequila and Mezcal are agave spirits that are distinctive products of Mexico, made in Mexico under Mexican law.

Cordials and liqueurs: flavored distilled spirits made by mixing or redistilling spirits with or over fruits, flowers, plants, juices or other natural flavors, containing at least 2.5% sugar by weight.

Scotch Whisky: produced in Scotland from water and malted barley (only whole grains of other cereals may be added); distilled at less than 94.8% ABV; matured only in oak casks of no more than 700 litres, only in Scotland, for at least three years; only water and plain caramel coloring may be added; minimum 40% ABV. Categories: Single Malt, Single Grain, Blended Malt, Blended Grain, Blended Scotch (single malt(s) blended with single grain(s)). Single Malt: one distillery, water and malted barley only, pot stills.
Protected Scotch localities: Campbeltown and Islay; protected regions: Highland, Lowland and Speyside.
Any maturation period or age on a spirit drink label refers to the youngest alcoholic component; Scotch age statements must be in years.

Cognac aging: the age is the youngest component of the blend. Cognac cannot be sold before at least two years of aging, without interruption, exclusively in oak. At least 2 years: VS ('3 Etoiles', 'Sélection', 'De Luxe', 'Very Special'); at least 4 years: VSOP ('Réserve', 'Vieux', 'Rare', 'Royal', 'Very Superior Old Pale'); at least 10 years: XO ('Hors d'âge', 'Extra', 'Extra Old' and others); 14 years or more: 'XXO', 'Extra Extra Old'; 6 years: 'Napoléon', 'Très Vieille Réserve' and others. Minimum 40% ABV. 'Fine Champagne' = Grande Champagne (minimum 50%) and Petite Champagne.
Cognac uses batch double distillation in two 'chauffes', completed no later than March 31 of the year after the harvest; no sugar or sulphites may be added during fermentation.
Only blue agave (Agave tequilana Weber) is permitted for Tequila. The Appellation of Origin covers 181 municipalities in five states: Jalisco, Michoacán, Guanajuato, Nayarit and Tamaulipas.

Tequila 100% Agave: made from 100% blue agave sugars and bottled at origin. Tequila: at least 51% blue agave sugars, up to 49% other sugars, may be bottled outside the territory. Blanco: direct from the still, only adjusted with water. Joven/Oro: blend of white Tequila with rested, aged or extra-aged Tequila. Reposado must mature in oak or holm oak for at least 2 months, añejo at least one year, extra añejo at least 3 years; añejo and extra añejo in barrels of max 600 liters.

Pomace brandy or Marc brandy: brandy distilled from the skin and pulp of sound, ripe grapes or other fruit, after the withdrawal of the juice or wine. Grape pomace brandy may alternatively be designated 'grappa' or 'grappa brandy'.
Beer (Intro): yeast can also provide aromas and flavors to beer. Hops: many different varieties produce a wide range of flavors and aromas. Water: clean water is essential to the brewing process.

Sake (Intro): koji-kin is a special mold native to Asia. Diverse yeast strains provide unique aromas and flavors. Water is an important component of final flavor; each producer has its own unique water source (the Court's text says 'each sake distillery').

Learning outcomes, Introductory Sommelier Course. BEER: 'After studying this section, a student will know what beer is, its primary ingredients and what they contribute to a beer, the difference between an ale and lager, and examples of each.' (p83) SAKE: 'After studying this section, a student will know what sake is, where it's from, its main ingredients, and the basics of how it is made. A student will learn a quality classification exists and will be able to recognize quality categories.' (p86) SPIRITS & LIQUEURS: 'After studying this section, a student will learn basics of spirit and liqueur production including the base ingredients, flavors, and location of production for important spirits of the world.' (p88)
Course Section 11 resources: Curriculum Guide, chapter in workbook, section quiz (for Beer, Sake, and Spirits and Liqueurs). Exam content lists Beer Basics, Sake Basics and Spirits Basics.

keyPoints.line: gives the sugar, plus color, flavor and body.

read.bigIdea: Beer is grain, water, hops and yeast.
read.where:
Beer is a fermented drink made from cereal grains, mainly **barley**. Rice, corn, wheat and oats are used too.

The grain’s starch has to become sugar before it can ferment. The Court names the steps as **germination**, **malting** and **fermentation**.

stops.name: Malt
stops.text: **Malt** gives the sugar for fermentation. It also brings color, flavor, body and mouthfeel.

stops.name: Hops
stops.text: **Hops** are the flowering cone of the hop vine. They add aroma, flavor and bitterness to balance the malt’s sweetness, and they are a natural preservative. Many varieties give a wide range of flavors and aromas.

stops.name: Yeast
stops.text: **Yeast** eats the malt sugars and makes alcohol. The type of yeast decides whether the beer is an **ale** or a **lager**. It can add aromas and flavors too.

stops.name: Water
stops.text: Water makes up **90% or more** of a beer. Clean water is essential.

keyPoints.line: use top-fermenting yeast: more fruit and spice.
use bottom-fermenting yeast: clean and crisp.
is a lager that started in the Czech Republic.
is a German wheat ale with banana and clove notes.
is a sour Belgian wheat beer made with wild yeast.

read.bigIdea: The yeast decides: ale or lager.
read.where:
**Ales** use **top-fermenting** yeast. They ferment warm and fast, and show more fruit and spice.

**Lagers** use **bottom-fermenting** yeast. They ferment cool and slow, and taste clean and crisp.

stops.name: Britain and Ireland
stops.text: Britain gives **Pale Ale**, **IPA** and **Porter**. Ireland gives **Irish Dry Stout**: black and roasty, often like coffee, and creamy on a nitro pour.

stops.name: Belgium
stops.text: **Lambic** is sour and fermented by wild yeast and bacteria. **Witbier** is a hazy wheat ale spiced with coriander and dried orange peel.

stops.name: Germany
stops.text: **Hefeweizen** is a wheat ale with banana and clove. **Pilsner**, **Bock**, **Doppelbock** and **Oktoberfest** are German lagers.

stops.name: Czech Republic
stops.text: **Pilsner** started here. Pilsner Urquell was first brewed in **Plzeň** in 1842.

read.visualIntro: Every style lands on one side:
read.mixup: **Hefeweizen** is a German wheat ale. **Witbier** is a Belgian wheat ale, spiced with coriander and orange peel.
read.sayIt: It’s a German wheat beer, with banana and clove notes.

read.bigIdea: Sake is brewed from polished rice.
read.where:
Sake is a fermented drink made from rice, and most of it is made in Japan. It uses special **sake rice** (not table rice), **koji**, yeast and water. Some styles also get **brewer’s alcohol**.

**Koji-kin** is a mold sprinkled over steamed rice. It turns starch into sugar while yeast turns that sugar into alcohol, at the same time: **parallel fermentation**. The Court gives sake as typically **15-22% ABV**. Different **yeast** strains give different aromas, and **water** shapes the final flavor: each brewery has its own source.

stops.name: Junmai
stops.text: **Junmai** means no alcohol was added.

stops.name: Honjozo
stops.text: Rice polished to **70% or less**, with a little neutral spirit added.

stops.name: Ginjo
stops.text: Rice polished to **60% or less** and fermented at low temperature. Fruity aroma, light flavor.

stops.name: Daiginjo
stops.text: Rice polished to **50% or less**, also fermented at low temperature. Add **Junmai** to either name and no alcohol was added.

stops.name: Two more words
stops.text: **Nigori** is cloudy sake. **Namazake** is unpasteurized.

read.visualIntro: Lower number, more of the grain milled away:
read.mixup: **Junmai** has no added alcohol. **Honjozo** adds a little neutral spirit.
read.sayIt: This is a Ginjo. It’s best served chilled.

video.title: How a Pot Still Works | Distiller

keyPoints.line: boils a fermented liquid and condenses the vapor.
work one batch at a time.
run nonstop. Coffey’s 1831 still led to grain whisky.
(US) comes off the still at 95% ABV or higher.

read.bigIdea: Distilling makes a fermented drink stronger.
read.where:
A spirit starts as a fermented liquid. It is boiled, and the vapor is condensed back into a **concentrated alcoholic liquid**.

The Court tests the basics of distillation and the **base ingredient** of each common spirit.

stops.name: Pot still
stops.text: **Single malt Scotch** must be distilled in batches in **copper pot stills**. The Court lists **Irish whiskey** as distilled three times in a pot still, and Scotch two times. **Cognac** is double distilled in batches.

stops.name: Column still
stops.text: In 1831 **Aeneas Coffey** invented the **Patent Still**. It made continuous distillation possible and led to **grain whisky**. The Court says vodka and gin are commonly made in continuous stills.

stops.name: US strength rules
stops.text: **Vodka** is neutral spirit distilled at **95% ABV (190 proof)** or higher, and is not aged in wood. Whisky, brandy and rum are distilled below 95% and bottled at **40% ABV** or more.

read.visualIntro: What each spirit is made from:
read.mixup: **Cognac** is distilled twice in a pot still. **Armagnac** is distilled once in a continuous still.

video.title: From Grain to Glass: How Scotch Whisky is Made

keyPoints.line: is at least 51% corn, aged in charred new oak.

read.bigIdea: Whisky is distilled from grain, then aged in oak.
read.where: Under US law, **whisky** is distilled from a fermented mash of grain and stored in oak barrels. The Court’s table covers **bourbon**, **Tennessee**, **Canadian**, **Irish** and **Scotch**.

stops.name: Bourbon
stops.text: At least **51% corn**, distilled at 160 proof or less, and stored in **charred new oak**. No added color or flavor. It must be made in the US. Most is made in **Kentucky**, but that isn’t required. **Straight bourbon** ages at least **2 years**.

stops.name: Tennessee
stops.text: Also at least 51% corn. The Court lists **filtering through maple charcoal** as its distinct step.

stops.name: Scotch
stops.text: Made from water and **malted barley**, then aged in oak casks of 700 liters or less, in Scotland, for at least **3 years**. Peat fires that dry the barley give the smoke. The age on the label is the **youngest** whisky in the bottle.

stops.name: Irish and Canadian
stops.text: **Irish** whiskey is barley, distilled three times in a pot still. **Canadian** whisky uses corn, wheat, rye or barley, typically in a continuous still, and ages at least **3 years** in oak.

read.mixup: **Bourbon** and **Tennessee whiskey** are both at least 51% corn. Tennessee adds maple charcoal filtering.
read.sayIt: If you like smoke, try an Islay Scotch.

keyPoints.line: is grape brandy from France’s Cognac region.

read.where:
Under US law, **brandy** is distilled from the fermented juice, mash or wine of fruit, or from what’s left of it (the residue).

**Cognac** is grape brandy distilled only in France’s Cognac region, mainly from **Ugni Blanc**. It is double distilled in a **pot still** and aged in French oak. Distilling must end by **March 31** after the harvest.

stops.name: Cognac
stops.text: It can’t be sold before **2 years** in oak. **VS** means at least 2 years, **VSOP** 4, **Napoléon** 6, **XO** 10 and **XXO** 14 or more.

stops.name: Armagnac
stops.text: Grape brandy distilled **once** in a unique **continuous still**, then aged in French oak.

stops.name: Calvados
stops.text: Made from **apples and pears**. Distilled twice in a pot still (some use a continuous still), then aged in French oak.

stops.name: Grappa and Marc
stops.text: **Pomace brandies**, distilled from the grape skins and pulp left after the juice or wine is drawn off. Grappa is Italian; Marc is French. They are generally **not aged**.

stops.name: Eaux de vie de fruits
stops.text: Brandies made from fruit such as **raspberry**, **cherry** and **pear**. Generally **not aged**.

read.visualIntro: The label tells you the youngest brandy’s age:
read.mixup: **Fine Champagne** on a Cognac label means Grande Champagne (at least 50%) plus Petite Champagne. It’s a Cognac term, not a sparkling wine.
read.sayIt: This is a VSOP, so the youngest brandy in it is at least four years old.

read.bigIdea: Tequila and mezcal are agave spirits from Mexico.
read.where:
Under US rules, **Tequila** and **Mezcal** must be made in Mexico. Tequila may only use **blue agave**. Its appellation covers 181 municipalities in five states: **Jalisco**, Michoacán, Guanajuato, Nayarit and Tamaulipas.

**Tequila 100% Agave** uses only blue agave sugars and is bottled in the appellation. Plain **Tequila** needs at least **51%** blue agave sugars.

stops.name: Blanco
stops.text: Straight from the still, only adjusted with water.

stops.name: Joven
stops.text: Blanco blended with aged Tequila.

stops.name: Reposado
stops.text: Rested in oak for at least **2 months**.

stops.name: Añejo
stops.text: Aged at least **1 year**, in barrels of 600 liters or less.

stops.name: Extra Añejo
stops.text: Aged at least **3 years**, in barrels of 600 liters or less.

read.visualIntro: Tequila and mezcal side by side:
read.mixup: **Reposado** rests at least 2 months in oak. **Añejo** ages at least 1 year.
read.sayIt: A Reposado has rested in oak for at least two months.

video.title: WSET 3 Minute Spirit School - Vodka, Mia Johansson, Bar Owner & Manager

keyPoints.line: is neutral spirit, not aged in wood (US rule).
takes its main flavor from juniper berries.
is distilled from sugar cane juice, syrup or molasses.
are flavored spirits with at least 2.5% sugar (US).
Triple Sec and Grand Marnier are orange liqueurs.

read.bigIdea: Know what each spirit is made from.
read.where: The Court tests what each common spirit is made from. Vodka, gin and rum can be made anywhere in the world.

stops.name: Vodka
stops.text: Commonly made from grain, but it **can be anything**. In the US it is distilled at 95% ABV or higher and never aged in wood. The Court says it is commonly distilled **many times in a continuous still** to remove any flavors.

stops.name: Gin
stops.text: Neutral grain spirit flavored with botanicals. **Juniper berries** must give the main flavor. In the US, gin made only by distillation may be labeled **Distilled**, **Dry**, **London** or **Old Tom**. The Court lists it as made in a **continuous** still.

stops.name: Rum
stops.text: Distilled from **sugar cane** juice, syrup or **molasses**. Traditionally Caribbean, but it can be made anywhere. The Court’s styles are light, dark, aged and spiced. **Cachaça** is rum from Brazil. It can be made in a **continuous or pot** still.

stops.name: Liqueurs
stops.text: Spirits flavored with fruits, flowers, plants or other natural flavors, with at least **2.5% sugar** under US rules. Orange: **Triple Sec**, **Cointreau**, **Grand Marnier**. Coffee: **Kahlúa**, **Tia Maria**. Whiskey: **Drambuie**, Glayva, Irish Mist. Also on the Court’s list: **St. Germain** (elderflower) and **Canton** (ginger).

read.visualIntro: The Court’s liqueur list, by flavor:
read.mixup: **Drambuie** is a whiskey liqueur. **Kahlúa** is a coffee liqueur.
